reasons: frontend/src/lib/format.test.ts tests money, FTE, bands, percent and share of effort.
Several other formatters have no direct test in the files shown.
I did not run these tests in this review.

terms.meaning: full time equivalent, one person working full time for one year
the digits that carry meaning, counted from the first non-zero digit
a table that walks from gross benefit down to the net result

depends_on: the browser locale support for en-GB number formatting

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Rule that every figure carries a unit
sections.what: The header says every figure shown carries its unit, and that no path emits a bare number.
sections.watch_out: New formatters should follow this rule.

sections.name: money
sections.title: Money with its currency code
sections.what: Shows the currency code first, then the amount with thousands separators. Amounts under one hundred keep up to three significant digits, and larger amounts round to whole units.
sections.why: The comments say rounding once turned a real sub-unit cost into a whole unit, and made a small nonzero cost look free.
sections.watch_out: The one hundred threshold and the three significant digits define the rule. Changing either changes how small costs look.

sections.name: fte
sections.title: FTE with fixed decimals
sections.what: Shows a full time equivalent figure with a fixed number of decimal places, two by default.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code beyond the unit label.
sections.watch_out: The default is two places, so callers that need a different precision must pass it.

sections.name: fteMonths
sections.title: Effort in FTE-months
sections.what: Shows effort in FTE-months, with up to one decimal place.
sections.why: The comments say an earlier layout printed months with a stray FTE after them, which left the reader unsure whether the figure was a duration or an effort.
sections.watch_out: This shows effort, not duration. Use the months formatter for durations.

sections.name: months
sections.title: Duration in months
sections.what: Shows a duration in months with up to one decimal place.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.

sections.name: hours
sections.title: Elapsed hours
sections.what: Shows hours with the word elapsed, so the reader knows the figure is waiting time, not effort.
sections.why: The header of the process view says elapsed time is not effort, and mixing them double counts.
sections.watch_out: Use this only for elapsed time. Using it for effort would be a category error.

sections.name: days
sections.title: Source age in days
sections.what: Shows source age in days, with up to one decimal place.
sections.why: The comments say a bare number beside the half-life would leave the reader guessing its unit.

sections.name: quantity
sections.title: Counts with the record's own unit
sections.what: Shows a count followed by the unit name the record supplies, such as programmes or notifications.
sections.why: The comments say different counted things are not comparable, so the unit has to come from the record.
sections.watch_out: The caller must pass the unit. It is not guessed here.

sections.name: multiplier
sections.title: Widening factor with a times sign
sections.what: Shows a factor with two decimal places followed by a times sign.
sections.why: The comments say a bare number beside the word widened reads as an amount rather than a ratio.

sections.name: percent
sections.title: Fraction shown as a percent
sections.what: Turns a value between 0 and 1 into a percentage with one decimal place by default.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The input must be a fraction. A value already in percent would show a hundred times too large.

sections.name: shareOfEffort
sections.title: Share of effort as a percent
sections.what: Shows a share with the words of effort after it, so the denominator is clear.
sections.why: The comments say every share in the schema is a share of effort, not of steps or elapsed time.

sections.name: band
sections.title: Low, base and high range
sections.what: Shows the base value followed by the low and high values in brackets, each formatted by the unit function passed in.
sections.why: Keeps all three ends of a range in the same units.
sections.watch_out: The caller chooses the unit function. A wrong one mislabels all three values at once.

sections.name: score
sections.title: Score out of a total
sections.what: Shows a score with a slash and the total it is out of, five by default.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: The default total is five. A scale of another size must pass its total.

sections.name: ratio
sections.title: Three-decimal ratio
sections.what: Shows a number to three decimal places with no unit.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code.
sections.watch_out: This is the one formatter with no unit, which goes against the header rule, so check any new use of it.

sections.name: isoDate
sections.title: Date or missing note
sections.what: Returns the date text, or the phrase that no publication date was recorded when there is none.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code, though the wording suggests a missing date should be visible.
sections.watch_out: Despite the name, it does not check that the date is in a valid format.

summary: Formats numbers and text for display so that every figure shows its unit, and money shows its currency.
purpose: Keeps the pages from showing a bare number that a reader could misread, and keeps small costs visible rather than rounded to zero.
why: The header says a figure without its unit is unreadable next to one in another currency, and the reader cannot tell the system refused to add them.
how: Each function takes a number and returns text with its unit attached. Money rounds to whole units above one hundred, keeps three significant digits below that, and puts the minus sign after the currency code.
inputs: Numbers, plus a currency code or a unit name where needed. Some functions take a formatter for each end of a range.
outputs: Strings such as a currency amount, a percentage, an FTE figure or a score.
risks: The one hundred unit threshold and the three significant digits are the rule. Changing either changes how small costs look. The ratio function is the one formatter that shows no unit, which is an exception to the header rule.
debug: If a cost shows as rounded or as free, check the money function. If a unit is missing, check which formatter the page called.
